slides.text: November 26-27, 1933. Gandhi moves through the village circuits of Chhattisgarh — Tamora, Devri, Kurud and beyond. The places the cities cannot reach. The people the cities cannot speak for. The real India, receiving The Mahatma.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: A rural road in Chhattisgarh's Mahasamund region — Sal trees on both sides, Gandhi's motor in the distance, villages visible across the fields. The village circuit as pilgrimage. Morning light, warm and golden. The real India waiting ahead.

slides.text: The village circuit of November 26-27 was not planned for large public meetings. It was planned for small encounters — village assemblies, Harijan community meetings, temple visits, conversations in courtyards. The intimate Gandhi, not the platform Gandhi.
slides.visualDescription: The village circuit in its intimacy — Gandhi seated in a village courtyard, not on a stage. A small gathering of twenty or thirty people. No podium. No microphone. Just Gandhi on the ground with the people of a village that rarely sees leaders of any kind.

slides.text: The motor left Raipur early in the morning of November 26. Mahadev Desai beside Gandhi, notebook ready. Meera Ben in the group. The countryside opening up around them — the flat agricultural plains of Mahasamund, the distant line of forest.
slides.visualDescription: The early morning departure from Raipur — Gandhi's motor moving through the awakening countryside. Mahadev Desai with his notebook. Meera Ben looking out the window. The Mahasamund plains stretching ahead. A working day beginning in the manner of all working days: with movement.

slides.text: The first stop: Tamora — which Gandhi had already decided to name Gandhigram. The village that had stood for seventeen days against British lathis and bayonets in the 1930 Jungle Satyagraha. Gandhi's first village circuit stop as a pilgrimage to courage.
slides.visualDescription: Tamora village receiving Gandhi's motor — the village assembled in its entirety. The same faces that stood before bayonets in 1930, now welcoming the man who heard their story and came. The village as a site of proved courage. Gandhi as its witness and witness's witness.

slides.text: At Tamora: the meeting with Amar Singh and his wife, who had shouted Gandhi's name while being beaten. The meeting with Dayavati, who had stood before the rifle. Gandhi sitting with each of them individually — not as a Mahatma but as a student of their courage.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi seated individually with Amar Singh and wife, then with Dayavati. Small, personal meetings. No crowd, no stage. Gandhi's face: the quality of attention that makes the person speaking feel they are the only person in the world. The listener as the greatest honour.

slides.text: Gandhi declared Tamora as Gandhigram. The village workers made the sign. Gandhigram Tamora. A renaming that travelled through the village like music — each person saying it to themselves, testing the sound, feeling what it meant to be so acknowledged.
slides.visualDescription: The Gandhigram renaming in Tamora — the sign being made and placed. Gandhi watching. The village saying the new name: Gandhigram Tamora. The private sound of a name being adopted. The village's identity shifting to include this recognition. Pride without boasting.

slides.text: The Harijan community of Tamora received Gandhi separately — their own meeting, their own conversation. What untouchability had cost them daily, what they hoped for, what they had understood from the 1930 Satyagraha about their own capacity to resist injustice.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi with the Harijan community of Tamora — seated with them in their quarter. Their meeting separate from the general Tamora meeting. Gandhi listening to their specific experience of untouchability, their specific losses, their specific aspirations. The particularity of dignity.

slides.text: The Tamora meeting also included the temple question — as it would at every stop of the village circuit. Had any temple opened its doors to Harijans? If not, would the community consider it? Gandhi not commanding — asking. The question itself as the intervention.
slides.visualDescription: At Tamora — Gandhi asking about the temple. The village assembly discussing. Some in favour. Some resistant. The conversation itself as the change agent — these people had never publicly discussed this before. Gandhi's question forcing the discussion into the open.

slides.text: The motor moved on from Tamora to the next village. Then the next. Each village a variation on the same meeting: the public gathering, the Harijan meeting, the temple question, the Harijan Sevak Sangh collection. The circuit as a method, not just a journey.
slides.visualDescription: The motor moving between villages — Tamora to the next stop, then the next. The circuit as a systematic method: each village the same structure, each village a different response. Gandhi applying the same approach to different soils and seeing different flowers.

slides.text: Devri village — a community of Chamars, the leather-working community considered untouchable. Gandhi arrived and treated it as the most important stop on his circuit. Ate with them. Spoke with them for two hours. Left them with a different understanding of their own value.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi arriving at Devri — a Chamar village. The community assembled, uncertain of what to expect from a visit by the Mahatma. Gandhi sitting on the ground with them. Two hours of conversation. His message: your work is not your shame. Your labour is the foundation of the economy.

slides.text: Gandhi at Devri: 'The leather you work is worn by kings. The shoes on the British viceroy's feet were made by hands like yours. There is no untouchability in the labour that holds up the entire society. There is only injustice in the law that calls it so.'
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at Devri making his argument to the Chamar community — the leather workers who are called untouchable. His words: your work is what kings wear. The logic: the economy rests on their labour while their dignity is denied. The absurdity of untouchability made rational.

slides.text: The Devri community had never received a visitor of Gandhi's standing. They had expected him to remain at a distance, to speak from afar. When Gandhi sat down on the ground in their quarter and asked to eat with them, some wept before they could speak.
slides.visualDescription: The Devri community's reaction to Gandhi sitting with them — first surprise, then disbelief, then some weeping. The accumulated weight of generations of being told you are too polluted for human contact, met by a man who sits on your ground and asks to share your food.

slides.text: The food Gandhi ate at Devri — simple, prepared by Chamar women. He ate it with the same appetite and gratitude he ate anywhere. The Devri women watching him eat their food as if they could not quite believe it was happening. The ordinary miracle of being treated as human.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi eating the food prepared by the Chamar women of Devri — simple food on a simple plate. The women watching from a distance, then moving closer. His appetite and gratitude real, unperformative. The women's faces: the disbelief of people whose food has never been accepted.

slides.text: At Devri, Gandhi also asked about the children's schooling. Were they in schools? Were they in separate schools? Were they turned away? The education question as inseparable from the dignity question. The Harijan child excluded from learning is doubly robbed.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi asking about the Devri children's schooling. The answers: some in separate schools, some turned away, some not going at all. Gandhi noting each answer carefully. Education as the next frontier after temple entry and community dignity. The Mahadev Desai notebook filling.

slides.text: Kurud village — where the most dramatic event of the village circuit occurred. The caste Hindu community of Kurud, in Gandhi's presence, opened the temple doors to Harijans. The doors that had been closed for perhaps centuries, opened in one afternoon.
slides.visualDescription: Kurud village — the old temple at its center. The caste Hindu community assembled. Gandhi present as witness. A discussion. Then: the decision. The temple committee agreeing. The head priest stepping forward. The doors beginning to open. Light pouring from the interior.

slides.text: The Harijan families of Kurud who had never entered the temple — who had worshipped at its outer walls for generations — were called forward. They walked to the entrance. They stepped across the threshold. The first crossing. The moment that changes a village's relationship with itself.
slides.visualDescription: The Harijan families of Kurud walking toward the open temple door — slowly, disbelievingly. The threshold. The first foot crossing it. Then another. Then a family entering. The interior receiving them as it receives anyone: with its stone floor and its lamp and its silence.

slides.text: Gandhi stood at the side and watched. He did not lead the Harijans in. He did not open the doors himself. He had created the conditions — his presence, his question, his moral weight — but the community had made the choice. He stood witness to their freedom, not as its author.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the edge of the temple courtyard — watching the Harijan families enter without him. His posture: the posture of a witness, not a leader. He created the conditions. They made the choice. He stands to see it. The distinction between enabling and doing.

slides.text: The caste Hindu community of Kurud who opened the temple door — they are the unnamed heroes of this episode. The people who did the hard thing: overcame their conditioning, overcame their traditions, and opened a door. Without them, Gandhi's presence changes nothing.
slides.visualDescription: The caste Hindus of Kurud — unnamed in history, known only as the community that chose to open the door. Their faces: some resolute, some uncertain, all committed to what they had decided. The opening of a door as the hardest possible act of self-transformation.

slides.text: After the temple opening at Kurud, Gandhi spoke briefly. He thanked the community. He said: you have done today what should have been done long ago. The delay was not your shame — it is the shame of the system that taught you to close this door. Opening it begins the repair.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi speaking after the Kurud temple opening — his words of gratitude and challenge. He thanks them. He names the delay not as their shame but as the system's shame. He calls the opening a beginning, not an ending. The repair that takes generations to complete starting now.

slides.text: The Harijan Sevak Sangh collection in the village circuit — in every village, people giving what they could to the cause of Harijan uplift. Small amounts from people who had small amounts. Each coin from a village more significant than large amounts from cities.
slides.visualDescription: The fund collection in the village circuit — not the large amounts of Raipur and Bilaspur, but small coins from small pockets in Tamora, Devri, Kurud. Gandhi receiving each with equal gratitude. The small coin as equal proof of commitment. The village's generosity unmeasured by amount.

slides.text: At each village, Mahadev Desai recorded: who was there, what was said, what was decided, what was given. The notebook filling with the evidence of the circuit — the names the history books will not record, the acts the monuments will not mark.
slides.visualDescription: Mahadev Desai's notebook — pages filling with names, amounts, acts. The most complete record of what happened in the Chhattisgarh village circuit. The historian in the group doing the work of preservation. The notebook as the archive that makes this story possible to tell.

slides.text: Thakkar Bapa — the welfare worker who had devoted his life to tribal uplift — made specific notes in each village about what practical support the Harijan Sevak Sangh could provide. The circuit was not only Gandhi's moral presence but practical assessment of need.
slides.visualDescription: Thakkar Bapa in the village circuit — making practical assessments. What does this community need? What can the Harijan Sevak Sangh provide? The circuit as field assessment as well as moral intervention. Gandhi and Thakkar Bapa as complementary: the spirit and the practical.

slides.text: The November 26-27 village circuit covered a remarkable amount of territory. Each stop adding to the picture of what Chhattisgarh's villages needed, what they had, what they had been doing. Gandhi as the first national leader to systematically visit this region's villages.
slides.visualDescription: The village circuit mapped — the territory covered on November 26-27. The distances. The number of villages. The systematic coverage. Gandhi as the first national figure to take this kind of sustained personal tour of rural Chhattisgarh. The map as proof of care.

slides.text: What the villages gave Gandhi: the ground-level truth of the freedom movement and the Harijan cause. Not the polished picture of the city meetings but the raw reality of village India — its courage, its poverty, its complexity, its readiness.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi absorbing the village circuit's intelligence — the ground-level truth that cities cannot provide. The Harijan reality in the villages starker, more complex, more urgent than in the cities. Gandhi's notebook — through Mahadev Desai — filling with what the villages know.

slides.text: The village circuit taught Gandhi something he already knew but needed to relearn: that the freedom movement's real foundation was not in the courtrooms and congress halls but in the fields and courtyard gatherings of villages like Tamora, Devri, and Kurud.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi in a village courtyard — small gathering, no stage. The contrast with Victoria Garden's one lakh visible in his face. This is also necessary. This is also real. The village as the nation's actual foundation. Gandhi relearning in Chhattisgarh what Gokhale taught him in 1915.

slides.text: The village circuit ended as the sun set on November 27, 1933. The motor returning to Raipur for the last night. Tomorrow: November 28. Departure. The last morning in Chhattisgarh. The last time Gandhi will see this land.
slides.visualDescription: The motor returning to Raipur at sunset on November 27 — the last day of the village circuit. The Chhattisgarh sky in deep orange and red. Gandhi in the back seat. The land passing. He does not know this is his last sunset in this place. The land receiving him for the last time.

slides.text: Dayavati of Gandhigram Tamora — the woman who stood before the rifle. She would continue her life in the renamed village, carrying the weight of what she had done in 1930 and what Gandhi had acknowledged in 1933. Her courage: permanent, undefeated.
slides.visualDescription: Dayavati after Gandhi's visit — her life continuing in Gandhigram Tamora. The village renamed but otherwise unchanged in the ways that poverty keeps a village unchanged. Her courage still there. Her act still the village's defining story. Her name known in Tamora forever.

slides.text: The Chamar women of Devri who cooked for Gandhi — whose food he ate — continued their lives in Devri after the visit. The act of feeding him never forgotten by any of them. The day the Mahatma ate our food: the story told to grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
slides.visualDescription: The Chamar women of Devri in their homes after Gandhi's visit — continuing their daily lives. But something changed: the knowledge that their food was good enough for the Mahatma. The dignity of having fed him. The story carried forward to every generation that followed.

slides.text: The Kurud temple door that opened in November 1933 — did it stay open? Some doors opened by Gandhi's presence later closed again. Some stayed open. History does not always answer this question clearly. But the opening happened. That cannot be undone.
slides.visualDescription: The Kurud temple door — open in 1933. The question of what happened after hanging in the air. Some doors stayed open; some closed. This one: unknown. But the opening itself: permanent. What happened in November 1933 happened. History cannot take it back.

slides.text: The village circuit was two days long. In those two days, Gandhi's presence touched perhaps thirty villages — thirty communities who had the experience of Gandhi in their courtyard, Gandhi eating their food, Gandhi asking about their children and their Harijans.
slides.visualDescription: Thirty villages across the Mahasamund region — each one a point on the circuit map. Each one carrying the memory of Gandhi's presence. Thirty communities changed by two days of The Mahatma in their midst. The scale of what two days in a motor can accomplish.

slides.text: The village circuit was the part of Gandhi's visit that no history book adequately covers. The Raipur meetings, the Victoria Garden lakh — these are recorded. The villages: recorded only in Mahadev Desai's notebook and in the living memory of the people who were there.
slides.visualDescription: The contrast between recorded and unrecorded — the Victoria Garden meeting with its lakh photographed and noted, the village circuit known only through Desai's notebook and oral memory. The hierarchy of historical recognition. The villages always at the bottom of the archive.

slides.text: This book — Johar Gandhi — exists partly to give those villages their place in the record. Amir Hashmi's research: two to three years of finding descendants of the Satyagrahis, recording their memories, reconstructing what the official record omitted.
slides.visualDescription: The author's research made visible — Amir Hashmi traveling to villages like Tamora and Kurud and Devri, sitting with descendants, recording what was never officially recorded. The book as the archive the official history refused to maintain. The author as the village's historian.

slides.text: Tamora, Devri, Kurud — three villages that received Gandhi in November 1933. Three villages that are not in any national history of the freedom movement. Three villages that deserve to be. This episode is their monument.
slides.visualDescription: Tamora, Devri, Kurud — named on screen, their images shown. The monument they never received: this naming. The act of putting them in the record, even in a web series, as their claim on historical recognition. The names as monuments.

slides.text: The village circuit of November 26-27, 1933: a two-day tour through the heart of rural Chhattisgarh. A private Gandhi — not the platform orator, not the global icon — but the man who sat on the ground and listened. The Gandhi who made time for thirty villages.
slides.visualDescription: The private Gandhi of the village circuit — on the ground, listening, eating, asking questions. Not performing. Not orating. The most human version of the most famous human of his age. The Gandhi who chose villages when the cities were waiting. The choice itself as the statement.

slides.text: November 27, 1933. The last village on the circuit. The motor turns back toward Raipur. Tomorrow is November 28 — departure day. Gandhi has one more night in Chhattisgarh. One more morning. One more farewell.
slides.visualDescription: The motor leaving the last village of the circuit, turning toward Raipur. November 27's last light. One more night in Chhattisgarh. One more morning. Gandhi and the land in their last hours together, neither knowing it is the last. The final approach.

slides.text: What the village circuit meant: Gandhi chose to go where no leader goes — not because it was politically useful, but because the villages were where the need was greatest and the voices were quietest. The choice of the village over the city: Gandhi's clearest political statement.
slides.visualDescription: The political statement of the village circuit — Gandhi choosing rural Chhattisgarh when urban Chhattisgarh was also available. The choice as philosophy: go where the need is greatest. The Mahatma who walked to the margins because he understood they were the center.

slides.text: Two days in the villages. Thirty communities touched. One temple opened. One village renamed. Thirty plates of village food shared. The circuit complete. Next: Episode 7 — The Last Morning.
slides.visualDescription: The village circuit complete — the motor returning to Raipur at last light. Behind it: Tamora with its new name, Devri with its shared meal, Kurud with its open door. Thirty communities carrying something different than they had two days ago. Title: Episode 7 — The Last Morning.
